steps.title: Use a clean device, not the infected computer
steps.detail: Do everything from your phone or from a computer that shows no warning. Use it to read this plan, make calls and send messages.
steps.why: The attackers may be watching the infected computer and your email. A clean device keeps your next steps private.
steps.do_not: Do not type passwords, search the web or send email on the infected computer.

steps.title: Disconnect the infected computer from the network
steps.detail: Unplug its network cable and turn off its Wi-Fi. Leave the computer switched on.
steps.why: Ransomware spreads to other computers over the network. Cutting the connection stops it from reaching more of your files.
steps.do_not: Do not turn the computer off or restart it. Only turn it off if you cannot disconnect it from the network.

steps.title: Check your other computers
steps.detail: Look at every other computer, laptop and server for the same message, strange file names or files that will not open. Disconnect any that look affected.
steps.why: Ransomware often hits several machines at once. You need to know which ones are affected before you get help.

steps.title: Unplug your backups
steps.detail: Disconnect any backup drive or backup box (NAS) from computers and from the network. Put it somewhere safe.
steps.why: Attackers try to lock or delete backups too. A clean backup is often the fastest way to recover.
steps.do_not: Do not plug the backup into any computer until your IT contact says it is safe.

steps.title: Take a photo of the ransom message
steps.detail: Use your phone to take a clear photo of the screen, including any file names, amounts, deadlines and contact details shown.
steps.why: Investigators and your IT contact use these details to identify the ransomware and help you.

steps.title: Write down what happened and when
steps.detail: On paper or your phone, note the time you first saw the problem, who saw it, which computers are affected and what you have done so far.
steps.why: A clear timeline helps IT, your insurer and the police respond faster.

steps.title: Call your IT contact
steps.detail: Phone your IT person or IT company now. Tell them it looks like ransomware, which computers are affected and what you have done.
steps.why: Removing ransomware and restoring systems safely needs an expert.
steps.do_not: Do not try to remove the ransomware or unlock files yourself.

steps.title: Tell your staff by phone or text
steps.detail: Let staff know there is a computer problem and ask them not to use work computers or work email until you say so.
steps.why: This stops the problem from spreading. Phone and text avoid systems the attackers may be able to read.
steps.do_not: Do not send the warning from work email.

steps.title: Do not contact the attackers
steps.detail: Do not reply to the message, visit its links or call any number it shows. Leave every decision about the ransom note to your IT contact, insurer and law enforcement.
steps.why: The FBI does not recommend paying a ransom. Paying does not guarantee you get your files back and can lead to more attacks.

steps.title: Leave affected computers as they are
steps.detail: Keep the affected computers and files exactly as they are until your IT contact or investigators say otherwise.
steps.why: Investigators need the computers untouched to find out how the attackers got in.
steps.do_not: Do not wipe, reset or reinstall the computers, and do not delete any files.

steps.title: Call your insurance company
steps.detail: If you have cyber or business insurance, call their claims line and tell them you may have ransomware.
steps.why: Many policies require you to report quickly, and some insurers provide incident response experts.

steps.title: Report it to the FBI
steps.detail: From a clean device, file a report at ic3.gov. Include your timeline and the photo of the ransom message.
steps.why: Your report helps the FBI track attackers and may help you recover.

steps.title: Report it to CISA
steps.detail: From a clean device, report the incident at cisa.gov/report.
steps.why: CISA can offer free help and warn other businesses about the same attack.

steps.title: Change important passwords from a clean device
steps.detail: From a clean device, change the passwords for your email, bank and admin accounts. Turn on two-step sign-in where you can.
steps.why: Attackers often steal passwords before they lock files.
steps.do_not: Do not change passwords on the infected computer.

steps.title: Restore only with your IT contact
steps.detail: Let your IT contact decide when and how to restore your systems from clean backups.
steps.why: Restoring before the attackers are removed can lock your files again.
steps.do_not: Do not restore backups yourself before the cause has been found and fixed.
